list.listitem: Infective endocarditis (IE) should be suspected in a patient with bacteremia that has no clear source (especially if the patient has structural cardiac abnormalities, prosthetic valves, intravenous drug use, or intravenous catheters). A
Antimicrobial therapy is based on the sensitivity of the causative organism and is lifesaving. A
Initial empiric therapy should include vancomycin plus an aminoglycoside (with the addition of rifampin, if the patient has a prosthetic valve). B
Valve replacement/removal can improve survival in selected patients. B
Patients who have survived infective endocarditis will need antimicrobial prophylaxis before certain procedures. B

background.definition: Infective endocarditis is an infection of the lining of the heart chambers and heart valves caused by bacteria, fungi, or other infectious agents.

list.listitem: There are approximately 15,000 new cases of endocarditis each year in the United States.
Rates of infective endocarditis in persons with prosthetic valves or intravenous drug use are 100 times higher than in the general population.
Bacteria, especially Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species, are the most common causes of infective endocarditis.
When blood cultures are negative, more unusual causes must be considered. These include the HACEK organisms described in .
Intravenous catheters have emerged as the most common predisposing factor for endocarditis, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
Ulcerations on the valvular endothelial surface facilitate bacterial adherence.
Organisms in the bloodstream bind to small clots on the subendothelial surface. This activates cytokine production, resulting in progressive enlargement of the infected vegetation.
The prevention of catheter-associated endocarditis requires appropriate insertion and maintenance of intravascular catheters. B

Antimicrobial prophylaxis prior to dental, oral, respiratory, and esophageal procedures should be provided to persons who have prosthetic valves, congenital heart disease, previous infective endocarditis, and transplant-associated valvulopathy. B

Catheter-associated bacteremia is a primary cause of endocarditis in the modern era. Primary prevention methods include sterile insertion of indwelling intravascular devices and catheters. Intravascular catheters should be removed promptly when no longer needed. Peripheral intravenous catheters should be changed regularly to avoid infection.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is no longer recommended for dental procedures for most persons with structural heart defects. It is recommended for cardiac transplant recipients who develop valvulopathy. Prophylaxis is recommended only before dental procedures that "involve manipulation of gingival tissue or the periapical region of teeth or perforation of oral mucosa." They should also receive prophylaxis before procedures on the respiratory tract, infected skin, or musculoskeletal tissue. Prophylaxis is not recommended for nondental procedures such as transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) and GI or GU procedures.

Recommended prophylaxis is oral amoxicillin 2 g (50 mg/kg for children) 30 to 60 minutes before procedure. If unable to take oral medication, use 2 g intramuscular or IV ampicillin (50 mg/kg for children) or 1 g intramuscular or IV cefazolin or ceftriaxone (also 50 mg/kg for children). If allergic to penicillin or amoxicillin, alternatives include cephalexin 2 g (50 mg/kg for children), clindamycin 600 mg (20 mg/kg for children), or azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg (15 mg/kg for children). Finally, if penicillin allergic and unable to take oral medications use cefazolin or ceftriaxone 1 g IV or intramuscular (50 mg/kg for children) or clindamycin 600 mg intramuscular or IV (20 mg/kg for children).

The 2007 guidelines do not recommend prophylaxis prior to GI or procedures, for persons with mitral valve prolapse or other valvular conditions not mentioned above, or for ear piercing, tattooing, vaginal delivery, or hysterectomy.

Infective endocarditis should be suspected in a patient with bacteremia that has no clear source. Suspicion should be higher in patients with structural cardiac abnormalities, prosthetic valves, intravenous drug use, or intravascular catheters. A

Modified Duke criteria may be used to guide diagnosis, but that criteria predate modern and emerging molecular diagnostic methods. C They use blood cultures and echocardiography as the principle foundation of diagnosis. For "culture-negative" infective endocarditis, obtain serology for less common organisms and alert the laboratory to incubate blood cultures for HACEK organisms.

list.listitem: Numerous diagnostic criteria exist reflecting the relative infrequency of the diagnosis and the heterogeneity of the population affected by infective endocarditis.
The modified Duke criteria are commonly used in .

The modified Duke criteria predated most molecular assays for specific pathogens. These emerging diagnostic techniques may someday play an important role in the modern diagnosis of infective endocarditis.
Fever is present in up to 90% of patients and murmurs are present in approximately 85%.
Peripheral stigmata may occur, but are not as common as in the past. They include Janeway lesions, Osler's nodes, splinter hemorrhages, and conjunctival hemorrhages.
Emboli to major organs, including brain, lung, and spleen, occur in up to 30% of patients.
Three sets of blood cultures should be drawn (prior to antimicrobial therapy if possible). Blood cultures should continue to be drawn every 24 to 48 hours until the bacteremia is cleared.

A trial randomized 256 patients to single sampling strategy (SSS) for blood cultures (3 cultures at once) or multiple sampling strategy (MSS, 3 samples taken one hour apart). IE was diagnosed in 101 patients, and sensitivity (50% for SSS and 46% for MSS) and specificity (95% for both) were similar.

Transthoracic echocardiography is the initial test of choice. If results are normal and clinical suspicion remains high, a TEE should be performed.A repeat transesophageal echocardiogram can be considered if initial testing is negative and clinical suspicion remains high; a common interval is one week after initial testing.

In 1 study, a positive echocardiogram (vegetations, perivalvular abscess, moderate/severe perivalvular regurgitation, pseudoaneurysms, fistulae, valve dehiscence) had a positive and negative predictive value of 94% and 96%, respectively.

If initial blood cultures are negative and suspicion remains high, serum should be analyzed for Brucella, Bartonella, Coxiella, and Chlamydia species antibodies. The microbiology laboratory should be alerted to the possibility of HACEK organisms and will incubate blood cultures for extended periods. Fungal blood cultures should be considered.
Serum testing of C-reactive protein or procalcitonin has not been shown to aid the diagnosis of infective endocarditis.
See algorithm in .
Antimicrobial therapy should be appropriately matched to the sensitivity of the organism. A
Valve removal/replacement can improve survival in carefully selected patients. B

Early surgical intervention can decrease embolic events compared to conventional therapy in patients with left-sided endocarditis, large vegetations, and severe valve disease but no other urgent indications for surgery.

The choice of therapy depends on the sensitivity of the pathogen to antimicrobial agents. The American Heart Association has developed treatment recommendations endorsed by the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

Whenever possible, blood cultures should be obtained prior to starting antimicrobial therapy. While awaiting culture results, empiric therapy may be started. The decision to use empiric therapy and the choice of antimicrobial agent depend on the situation. However, it is prudent to include coverage for methicillin-resistant staphylococci in intravenous drug users, persons who have had intravascular catheters, and those with prosthetic valves.

The combination of vancomycin and an aminoglycoside provides coverage for staphylococci, most enterococci, and streptococci in patients with native valves (in patients with a prosthetic valve, rifampin should be added). Once blood culture results are available, empiric therapy should be appropriately modified.

For native valve endocarditis caused by highly penicillin susceptible viridans strep and strep bovis, aqueous crystalline penicillin G (12-18 million U/24 H continuously or in 4-6 divided doses) or ceftriaxone sodium (2 gm/24 h IV or IM in a single dose) are preferred. For strains of strep viridans and strep bovis that are relatively resistant to pencillin, penicillin (24 million U/24 hr) or ceftriaxone plus gentamicin is recommended. For staph infections in native valves, vancomycin is recommended for oxacillin resistant strains; for oxacillin sensitive strains, the combination of nafcillin or oxacillin plus gentamicin is recommended. For staph infections in prostethic valves, vancomycin plus rifampin plus gentamicin is generally recommended.

Treatment duration also depends on the pathogen and underlying morbidities. For S. aureus (the most common pathogen), treatment is usually given for 6 weeks. For viridans streptococci, shorter durations are used if the organism is highly susceptible. In prosthetic valve endocarditis, therapy in excess of 6 weeks and surgery is often required.

A quasi-experimental study compared outcomes in patients with endocarditis caused by enterococcus faecalis treated with gentamicin for 28 days before January, 2007 and those treated for only 14 days which became the standard duration after January, 2007. There was no difference in one year event free survival (66% vs 69%), and those receiving a longer duration of therapy had a somewhat greater decrease in GFR (11 vs 1 ml/min).

Outpatient intravenous therapy is appropriate with compliant patients whose insurance will cover this modality. Outpatient therapy usually requires a reliable support system in the home, easy access to the hospital, regular visits by a home infusion nurse, and careful supervision by an experienced physician.
One study found oral antibiotics for sensitive organisms to be non-inferior at 6 months to intravenous antibiotics for uncomplicated left sided endocarditis.

A systematic review identified four studies comparing oral with IV delivery of antibiotics (n=390 for outcome of treatment failure). There was no difference between groups for any individual study or in the meta-analysis (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.57).

Valve removal/replacement is indicated in patients with uncontrolled infection demonstrated by persistent bacteremia, in patients with hemodynamic compromise, and in those with fungal endocarditis. In some cases, surgery is performed for recurrent embolic events. Also consider surgery for patients with perivalvular extension, heart block, large abscess or extension of abscess.
Early surgical intervention has been shown to reduce embolic events. Compared with conventional therapy, this approach has not been shown to reduce mortality.
If one of the above indications is present, surgery is associated with a better outcome than medical therapy alone in patients with staphylococcal and prosthetic valve endocarditis.
Advanced age, presence of heart failure, and intracardiac abscess are independent risk factors for surgery.
Patients who have had infective endocarditis in the past will need antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures or procedures on the respiratory tract, musculoskeletal tissue, or infected skin. B
Without treatment, subacute bacterial endocarditis is highly fatal. Death occurs from sepsis, valvular dysfunction, or emboli.
In-hospital mortality rates vary by pathogen and according to host factors.
For the most common pathogen, S. aureus, in-hospital mortality ranges from 15% to 26% in most studies.

In complicated infective endocarditis on native valves, poor prognostic signs include abnormal mental status, moderate/severe heart failure, a causative agent other than viridans streptococci, and medical therapy without surgery.
Patients who have had subacute bacterial endocarditis should be aware of the guidelines for antibiotic prophylaxis.

list.listitem: Blood culture positive for IE Typical organisms isolated from 2 separate blood cultures and Streptococcus (viridans, bovis), community-acquired enterococcus, HACEK, or S. aureus OR Persistent bacteremia with less typical organisms that are associated with IE defined as at least 2 blood cultures at least 12 h apart or at least 3 blood cultures drawn at least 1 h apart OR Single positive culture for C. burnetii or antiphase 1 IgG antibody titer >1:800
